abstract: Abstract Diabetes mellitus is a group of chronic metabolic diseases worldwide that seriously threaten human health and increases the social and economic burden; underlying drivers of impaired healing include uncontrolled inflammation, repeated ischemia reperfusion injury, and neuropathy alongside infection risks. Macrophages orchestrate standard repair, exhibit sustained classical pro-inflammatory activation in diabetes, disrupting growth factor secretion, angiogenesis, and matrix regulation. Hyperglycemia mediated advanced glycation end products and reactive oxygen species heighten pattern recognition receptor stimulation, causing reduced alternative macrophage differentiation. Promising immunomodulation approaches redirecting their phenotypes to resolve inflammation and stimulate regeneration provides optimism. We discuss macrophage origination, polarization dynamics, diabetic wounds phenotypic imbalance, and critical microenvironmental disruptions perpetuating pathological function. Elucidating specific regulatory nodes upholding their activation states will inform intelligent targeting opportunities. Overall, infiltrating macrophages constitute indispensable yet amenable diabetic wound healing coordinators.

Highlights
Wound healing comprises of stages: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation, and remodelling. The wound microenvironment includes various cytokines and growth factors, extracellular matrix, oxidative stress, pH, microbiome populations, tissue oxygenation gradient, and other factors.
The ontogeny and polarization dynamics of macrophages underscore their indispensable roles as master regulators of repair processes, and macrophages orchestrate the wound healing in different phases.
In diabetic wounds, macrophages exhibit progenitor stage maturation anomalies, recruitment and transmigration impairments, maturation and phenotypic imbalance, substantial deficits in tissue repair function, immunometabolic disruption, and epigenetic rewiring.
Explore emerging therapies targeting macrophages and microenvironment.
Background
Skin injury elicits an intricately orchestrated series of cellular and molecular events to achieve wound closure and tissue repair [
1
,
2
]. Impaired healing, as manifested prominently in chronic diabetic wounds, remains a significant clinical challenge underscored by poorly understood pathophysiology [
1
]. Resident and recruited immune cells, especially macrophages, are pivotal in coordinating nearly all phases of wound healing through dynamic activation states and crosstalk with other cell populations [
3–6
]. Consequently, illuminating macrophage functional regulation in tissue repair processes has important implications for understanding dysfunctional healing.
Wound closure requires the coordinated efforts of various skin resident cells, circulating immune cells, cytokines, growth factors, and extracellular matrix (ECM) components [
1
]. This process progresses through hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling [
2
]. Macrophages critically regulate inflammation, clear apoptotic cells (ACs), and stimulate angiogenesis and matrix deposition, consequently orchestrating the transition between phases [
3
]. They originate from yolk sac progenitors (YSPs) during embryogenesis and bone marrow-derived monocytes in adults, the latter replenishing tissue macrophage populations during steady state and inflammation [
4
,
5
]. Their versatile functions depend on integrating microenvironmental cues that induce distinct polarization states—pro-inflammatory macrophages (M1) and anti-inflammatory macrophages (M2) subsets. M1 prevail early, releasing tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), IL-6, and IL-12, while M2 dominate later, producing IL-10 and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) [
1
,
2
,
6
].
Aberrant macrophage phenotype and persistence underpins impaired healing in many chronic wounds [
7
]. No wounds condition better epitomizes sustained M1 dysfunction than diabetes [
8
], the leading cause of nontraumatic limb amputations [
9
]. Diabetic wounds exhibit prolonged inflammation, exacerbated protease activity, reduced angiogenesis and ECM deposition, and increased apoptosis [
8–10
]. These manifestations partly stem from hyperglycemia induced reactive oxygen species(ROS), advanced glycation end products (AGEs), and augmented M1/M2 imbalance [
11
,
12
]. Promising immunotherapeutic developments targeting macrophages and the wounds microenvironment provide impetus to define regulators of macrophage activation for improved healing outcomes.
In this review, we detail the fine coordination of various immune cells and the cytokines they secrete during wound healing in healthy skin, focusing on macrophages [
8
]. In particular, the polarization mechanism of macrophages has been a hot topic in recent years, and we have described its abnormal manifestations in diabetic wounds [
8
] providing key molecular nodes to redress wound pathology. Finally, we discuss emerging therapeutic avenues centered on macrophages and their microenvironment of modifiers.
Review
The wound healing process and mechanisms in healthy skin
Tissue injury initiates a finely tuned healing program comprising overlapping phases—hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling [
2
,
13
]. This section describes cellular and molecular events governing each phase and their seamless coordination for skin integrity restoration.
Key phases of wound healing
Hemostasis begins immediately upon injury with vasoconstriction and fibrin clot formation to achieve hemostasis [
13
,
14
]. Thrombin generation activates platelets to release clotting factors, inflammatory mediators like platelet factor 4 (PF4), platelet derived growth factors (PDGFs), and TGF-β, PF4 inhibits angiogenesis. Simultaneously, PDGFs and TGF-β stimulate immune cells chemotaxis [
13–16
]. The ensuing inflammation phase comprises the early recruitment of neutrophils and later macrophages [
7
,
17
]. Neutrophils release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α, followed by AC clearance by M1 [
1
,
12
]. Transitioning to the proliferative phase, alternatively, activated M2 release vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs), PDGFs, fibroblast growth factors (FGFs), and TGF-β to stimulate angiogenesis, ECM deposition, and new tissue formation [
2
,
12
,
18–21
]. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) mediated ECM remodeling in the final phase enhances the structural integrity of the healed skin [
20
,
21
].
Cellular and molecular events in each phase
Hemostasis
Subendothelial collagen exposure upon injury initiates hemostasis via platelet adhesion through von Willebrand factor (vWF) and glycoprotein Ibα (GPIbα) interaction [
21
]. Activated platelets release α and dense granules containing adhesion molecules, clotting, chemokines, and mitogenic factors [
21
,
22
]. Released fibrinogen induces thrombocyte aggregation while activating the coagulation cascade [
14
,
23
], forming the platelet plug and fibrin-fibronectin meshwork [
21
,
24
]. Thrombin also elicits inflammatory responses by inducing endothelial cell release of C-C motif ligand 2 (CCL2), IL-6, and IL-8 chemokines [
1
,
2
,
14
,
24
,
25
]. Platelet α particles secrete PF4, a CXC chemokine inhibiting angiogenesis while promoting leukocyte recruitment [
15
,
22
,
26
,
27
].
Inflammation
Acute inflammation succeeds hemostasis to prevent infection and prepare the wound bed for repair [
1
,
27
]. Early neutrophils swarming peaks around 24 hours, mediated via complement activation and IL-1 release [
17
,
28
,
29
]. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) comprising deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins help destroy bacteria [
17
,
29
]. Macrophages dominate later, reaching peak numbers around 48–96 hours post injury. Monocytes recruited by macrophages’ chemokines like CCL2 and macrophage colony-stimulating factors (MCSFs) differentiate into M1 [
12
,
25
,
30
]. M1 debride cell debris and pathogens through phagocytosis and secrete TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-12, consequently activating t helper cell type 1 (Th1) immune responses [
31
]. Around Day 3, macrophages undergo a phenotype transition towards an M2 state, characterized by the release of IL-10, TGF-β, and VEGFs [
32–36
], M2 initiate inflammation resolution and tissue remodeling while suppressing t helper cell type 2(Th2) immune responses [
33
,
36
]. Notably, macrophage accumulation precedes the onset of the proliferative phase [
34
]. Selective macrophage depletion studies underscore their indispensability for the transition from inflammation to proliferation via regulating growth factors balance [
7
,
35
].
Proliferation
M2 growth factors like TGF-β, epidermal growth factors (EGFs), FGFs, and VEGFs stimulate the proliferation and migration of key cell types in this phase—keratinocytes, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells [
2
,
18
,
27
,
35
,
36
], activated keratinocytes at wound edges undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), releasing MMPs like collagenase and gelatinase to promote migration [
2
,
20
,
27
,
37
]. Fibroblasts proliferate and deposit new ECM enriched in fibronectin and hyaluronan [
20
,
21
,
38
,
39
].
VEGFs is a mitogen that stimulates the proliferation and migration of endothelial cells, and participates in the formation of neovascularization, followed by the extension of endothelial cells to surrounding tissues, which is highly mediated by integrin ανβ3 [
40
]. Pericytes with PDGF-β receptors are then recruited by PDGFs to surround the neovascularization, endowing the vessels with maturation and dormancy [
16
,
17
,
40
]. These cellular activities form granulation tissue—a highly vascularized tissue with immune cells and connective tissue elements [
17
,
27
,
41
]. Myofibroblasts finally facilitate wounds contraction before undergoing apoptosis, as collagen accumulation provides mechanical integrity [
41
,
42
].
Maturation and remodeling
This phase establishes scar tissue for long-term skin integrity via collagen remodeling to confer tensile strength [
27
,
38
,
41
,
42
]. The transition from predominant collagen III to collagen I synthesis occurs, although, unlike healthy skin, scar collagen is deposited in parallel bundles [
27
,
41
,
43
,
44
]. MMPs activity is also crucial—MMP-1 degrades collagen for cells migration, while MMP-9 facilitate angiogenesis by modifying basement membranes [
20
,
27
,
45
,
46
]. Myofibroblasts contraction and slowed keratinocytes proliferation signify the completion of the maturation phase as collagen production declines [
41
,
42
,
47
]. Dynamic ECM turnover continues, but stabilized collagen accumulation reduces wound area without losing strength [
20
,
41
,
48
] (
Figure 1
).

The immune microenvironment in wound healing
The wound microenvironment, comprising infiltrating immune cells, cytokines, growth factors, ECM, and physical factors, is pivotal for repair processes. Perturbations impeding the transition between healing phases manifest as chronic non-healing wounds [
1
,
7
,
19
,
27
]. This section explores immune cells and soluble mediators critically governing early inflammation and its timely resolution.
Cytokines and growth factors
Inflammation initiates upon IL-1 release from platelets, keratinocytes, and fibroblasts as an early warning signal [
1
,
49
,
50
]. The gene sequences of IL-1 family members are highly conserved, which can bind to toll-like receptors (TLRs) to mediate cell signaling and activate the nuclear factor kappa b (NFκB) pathway [
1
,
12
,
13
,
18
,
27
,
49
]. IL—1β needs NOD like receptors family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome complex to mediate its cleavage and maturation and further stimulate IL—1 production [
13
,
17
,
49–51
]. Other members exhibit dichotomous activities—IL-33 promotes ECM deposition while IL-18 enhances interferon-γ (IFN-γ) generation, and IL-22 significantly accelerates wounds re-epithelialization [
12
,
18
,
49
,
50
,
52
,
53
].
As inflammation progresses, infiltrating monocytes differentiate into macrophages [
34
]. Their predominant early M1 phenotype secretes TNF-α alongside IL-12 and IL-23 to stimulate Th1 [
1
,
17
,
18
,
31
,
41
,
54–56
]. M2 arise later, induced by IL-4 and IL-13 to produce IL-10 and TGF-β [
2
,
11
,
12
,
18
,
19
,
36
,
54–56
]. These cytokines provide negative feedback to resolve inflammation while enhancing tissue remodeling. Numerous studies highlight that cytokine levels must be precisely regulated across healing phases [
17
,
19
,
27
,
57
].
The PDGFs family plays indispensable mitogenic roles [
1
] for mesenchymal stem cells(MSCs) in the proliferative phase [
58
]. PDGFs receptor ligation stimulates fibroblasts and smooth muscle cell chemotaxis, proliferation, and matrix production [
59
]. Studies utilizing PDGF injections accelerated granulation tissue formation in rat wound models [
16
,
17
,
27
,
60
]. PDGF-BB recruits pericytes to stabilize nascent vascular networks by reducing endothelial proliferation [
16
,
17
,
40
,
58
,
61
].
VEGFs are essential in angiogenesis, lymphangiogenesis, and maintaining endothelial homeostasis. The VEGF-A isoform induces tip and stalk cells phenotype in sprouting nascent vessels via vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2), while VEGFR1 modulates its activity [
17
,
27
,
35
,
40
,
62
]. VEGF-C and –D binding VEGFR3 stimulates lymphangiogenesis [
41
,
63
], while placental growth factors (PLGFs) recruit monocytes and promote collateral vessel formation without side effects of abnormal angiogenesis [
27
,
40
,
41
,
64
].
The TFGs family is indispensable for cutaneous wounds repair by stimulating re-epithelialization, angiogenesis, and ECM synthesis [
2
,
21
,
27
,
65–73
]. TGF-β1 accelerates monocytes and fibroblasts infiltration and upregulates collagen production [
17
,
27
,
41
,
66
,
69
]. It also maintains the multipotency of progenitor cells, allowing expansion without differentiation [
67
]. Potent keratinocyte chemotactic (KC) properties of TGF-β1 hastens re-epithelialization by upregulating connective tissue growth factor [
17
,
27
,
68
,
69
]. Counter regulatory roles also exist as TGF-β3 predominates during scarless fetal repair [
65
] while TGF-β2 delays EMT [
27
,
37
,
70
].
From the submaxillary gland, EGFs were first isolated and shown to stimulate epidermal proliferation with applications in wound therapy [
27
,
71
]. EGFs accelerates MSCs migration without inducing it to differentiate [
27
,
72
,
73
]. In vivo evidence also indicates EGFs enable the transformation of adherent keratinocytes into motile phenotypes—a process sensitive to EGFs gradients rather than absolute concentrations [
27
,
73
]. Related family members like TGF-α, heparin-binding EGFs, and betacellulin exhibit similar activities.
FGFs represent ubiquitous peptides regulating wound angiogenesis and tissue remodeling [
27
,
74
,
75
]. Basic FGFs stimulates fibroblast migration by activating rho guanosine triphosphatase (Rho GTPase) and the NFκB pathway [
1
,
12
,
13
,
18
,
27
,
74–76
]. Various FGFs ligands modulate distinct repair phases—FGF7 and FGF10 promote keratinocytes organization [
74
,
77
,
78
], while FGF2 induces granulation tissue formation [
17
,
27
,
74
,
75
,
79
]. Unsurprisingly, deficient FGF signaling significantly impairs re-epithelialization and collagen organization [
27
,
41
,
69
,
74
,
78

Colony stimulating factors (CSFs) members, including macrophages, granulocytes, and GMs, primarily regulate emergency myelopoiesis. However, the development of macrophages and osteoclasts also depends on their signaling and stimulate multiple tissue proliferation [
80–85
]. Topical application of GMCSFs, can accelerate re-epithelialization in transgenic murine wounds while deficiency delayed crust formation [
12
,
13
,
18
,
27
,
69
,
80–82
]. Mechanistic studies revealed GMCSFs mediated IRF4 induction in macrophages, causing CCL17 mediated nociception and pain [
18
,
19
,
82–84
]. Various immune cell lineages, including T, B, and innate lymphoid cells, secrete GMCSFs, which orchestrates their proliferation and acquisition of effector phenotypes. In addition, GMCSFs can also increase the efficacy of ILs on target cells [
81
].
The TNFs superfamily member TNF-α exhibits dichotomous wound healing activities [
54
,
86
,
87
]. Although TNF-α stimulates TGF-β induced ECM production, its deficiency paradoxically impairs re-epithelialization despite improving other parameters [
2
,
27
,
54
,
65
,
66
,
69
,
86–88

76
,
86
,
87

89
,
90
] and leukocytes recruitment in skin wounds [
87
,

,

The ECM
The ECM provides structural scaffolding for cells while modulating their adhesion, migration, and communication [
20
,
48
,
92–94
]. ECM components like collagen, laminin, and fibronectin accumulate in granulation tissue, functioning through growth factor tethering, immune cells recruitment, and progenitor mobilization [
17
,
20
,
21
,
27
,
39
,
41
,
92
,
93
]. Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) mediate collagen bundle assembly and crosslinking for skin tensile strength acquisition [
21
,
41
,
42
,
93
]. In addition, GAGs are a component of the glycocalyx of macrophages and play an essential effect on the function of macrophages. Specific constituents like laminin-332 enable keratinocytes motility by regulating basement membrane MMPs activity [
20
,
21
,
41
,
66
,
95
]. Fibronectin and other provisional ECM components produced early following injury also influence inflammation resolution and fibrosis [
20
,
21
,
39
,
61
,

].
Myriad collagen subtypes exist, but type I and III fibrils form skin ECM bulk [
2
,
20
,
21
,
41
,
96
], although type VI collagen regulates macrophage function [
41
,
42
,
97
]. Collagen turnover involves concerted MMPs cleavage, while tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) provide counterbalance [
21
,
41
,
45
,
46
,
98
]. The intricate chemokine and matrix protein interplay spatiotemporal guides immune cells recruitment and behavior throughout repair phases. Disrupting ECM homeostasis thus compromises critical cell–cell communication pathways fundamental for healing.
Oxidative stress (OS)
Transient oxidative outbursts triggered upon injury activation have physiological immune signaling functions, but sustained stress disrupts healing [
99
,
100
]. Peroxide secretion also regulates macrophage phenotype changes during the transition between healing phases [
17
,
32
,
101
]. However, hyperglycemia associated generation of AGEs [
102
,
103
] and sustained ROS eventually cause growth factor and ECM abnormalities, leading to impaired healing [
99
,
103
]. Oxidative stress also perpetuates inflammation by activating NFκB while suppressing nuclear factor erythroid 2 related factor 2 (NRF2), augmenting protease activity [
1
,
12
,
13
,
18
,
76
,
86
,
101
,
103–105
]. Reinstating redox balance using antioxidant supplements or photobiomodulation helps mitigate pathological damage elicited by unrestrained OS [
101
,
103
,
106
,

Other local factors
Successfully restoring skin function upon injury necessitates spatiotemporal coordination among diverse cell types and biophysical elements. Multiple studies have explored how biophysical factors like potential of hydrogen (pH), microbiome populations, and tissue oxygenation gradients influence repair programs [
1
,
13
,
17
,
108–111
]. Low pH causes enzyme inactivation and impairs immune cell viability, while alkaline conditions accelerate re-epithelialization and collagen synthesis [
21
,
27
,
41
,
69
,
108
,
111
]. Imbalances in symbiotic microbial populations also delay healing by eliciting inflammatory disturbances [
109
,
112
]. Physiological transitions in oxygen tension promote vascular regression and ECM synthesis, but sustained hypoxia triggers pathological responses [
113
,
114
]. Developing stratified biomaterials replicating native wounds microenvironmental niches can potentially overcome the limitations of traditional wounds therapeutics.
Macrophages orchestrate wound healing
The mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS) exhibits remarkable functional plasticity in orchestrating all wound healing phases [
19
]. Their ontogeny, polarization dynamics, and multifaceted activities underscore their indispensable roles as master regulators of repair processes. Consequently, illuminating mechanisms governing their activation states provide crucial insights into designing immunotherapies targeting improved healing outcomes.
Origin, subsets and functions
Tissue resident macrophages (TRM) originate from YSP during embryogenesis, while postnatal monocyte-derived subsets replenish local populations [

]. Fate mapping studies reveal YS macrophages give rise to microglia, epidermal langerhans cells (LCs), intestinal macrophages, and heart macrophages while circulating Ly6C
high
monocytes differentiate into M1 [

]. Wound healing requires intricate collaboration between TRM and hematogenous recruited macrophages, although their relative contributions remain undefined [

].

Dynamic roles of macrophages in different wound healing phases

Conclusions
Chronic wounds represent a vast unmet clinical challenge, with diabetes afflicted patients alone exceeding 463 million currently. Pathological healing arises from perturbations across hematopoietic, vascular, stromal, and cutaneous compartments. Sustained inflammation forms the central mediator resulting from cellular dysfunction alongside hypoxia, acidosis, infection, and loss of coordination. Macrophages play an indispensable role in orchestrating transitions between the overlapping phases of repair. Their remarkable functional plasticity regulating inflammation, debridement, angiogenesis, and matrix remodeling underlies recruitment towards wound beds. Consequently, mechanistic insights into axes upholding macrophage homeostasis are essential for redressing healing impairments. We describe the current understanding of origins, activation states, signaling pathways, and effector functions allowing subsets specialization. Extensive redundancy nevertheless enables the preservation of tissue surveillance, pathogen response, and wound healing conducting roles despite temporary fluctuations. These are accentuated multifold in disorders like diabetes, where chronic inflammatory stimuli disrupt immune metabolic programming underlying phenotypic stability. Consequently, we elaborate on how hyperglycemia and concomitant OS impact hematopoietic development alongside promoting TLRs overstimulation. Growth factors perturbations also arise from ECM alterations and microbiome changes. Eventual manifestations include recurring ischemia, uncontrolled protease activity, and phenotypic imbalance. Repair phase coordinating abilities become compromised by the loss of angiogenic stimuli production, efferocytosis, and epithelialization routing. Unchecked neutrophils and alternatively activated macrophage persistence propagates self-sustaining chronic inflammation. Encouragingly, recent developments provide an armamentarium for tackling such multifactorial deficits by redressing local microenvironmental perturbations while providing immune recalibration. Biomaterial advances allow customizable cytokine, oxy-redox, and metabolic tuning to push macrophages and other participants toward pro-regenerative roles. Transplantation or endogenous activation of diverse progenitor lineages can simultaneously enhance tissue deposition and remodeling. Wound sites furthermore display heightened amenability for gene and RNA therapeutic administration. Overall, systems approach coopting immune metabolic networks, epigenetic plasticity, and functional biomaterials alongside emerging biotechnologies heralding an exciting era in regenerative medicine. We foresee future innovations arising from cross disciplinary efforts at the tissue material molecular interface. For instance, coupling immunomodulatory platforms with semiconductor sensing or M2 derived exosomes can enable closed loop immunological reprogramming. Machine learning guided cytokines formulations accounting for spatiotemporal nonlinear wound healing dynamics can fast track preclinical developments. Translational efforts would necessitate streamlining regulatory processes to fast track approval of synergistic cell materials combination products with favorable safety profiles. Specifically induced polyenergetic macrophages in patients exhibit enhanced efferocytic and cell matrix remodeling behavior, conditions that can overcome the autologous allogeneic mismatch. Therefore, successful research advances in these areas have far-reaching implications for reducing the healing pain of chronic intractable wounds, not just diabetic wounds.
